requirements.product_understanding: A rate-limiting service that enforces configurable request quotas (requests-per-minute) per tenant across a multi-tenant API platform. The system must distribute quota enforcement consistently across many stateless API gateway nodes, support per-endpoint override limits, and maintain sub-5ms p99 latency while ensuring no single point of failure for the entire platform.
users_and_use_cases: Platform tenants (API consumers): Configure their own request quotas and endpoint-specific overrides, make API requests that are subject to rate limiting
Platform ops: Manage tenant configurations, monitor rate-limiting performance, maintain system availability
functional: System must enforce configurable requests-per-minute quota per tenant across all API gateway nodes
System must support per-endpoint override limits for individual tenants
System must distribute rate-limit decisions consistently across stateless API gateway nodes
System must process rate-limit decisions with p99 latency under 5ms
System must not become single point of failure for the platform
System must handle 500,000 requests/sec across all tenants
System must support thousands of concurrent tenants
non_functional: Performance & scalability: Must process 500,000 requests/sec with p99 latency under 5ms; system must scale horizontally to handle tenant load distribution
Availability & reliability: 99.99% availability target implies maximum of 53 minutes downtime per year
Security & compliance: System must not store or process any regulated data (payment, health, PII) as this is a rate-limiting layer only
Maintainability & operability: System must be operable within $15,000/month budget with minimal operational overhead
Usability/compatibility constraints: System must support stateless API gateway nodes without requiring persistent state or coordination
assumptions: Assuming rate-limit decisions are based on tenant-level quotas with endpoint overrides, not complex policy rules
Assuming system will use distributed state management (e.g., Redis cluster) to avoid single point of failure
Assuming API gateway nodes will communicate with rate-limiting service via lightweight RPC or HTTP calls
Assuming tenant configuration changes are infrequent enough that caching is acceptable for performance
Assuming the $15,000/month budget covers all infrastructure and operational costs including monitoring and alerting
open_questions: What is the expected distribution of requests per tenant? (e.g., uniform vs. skewed)
What is the expected frequency of endpoint override changes?
What specific technologies or infrastructure are available for implementing distributed state management?
How will system monitoring and alerting be implemented within the $15,000/month budget?
What level of consistency is required for rate-limiting decisions across distributed nodes? (strong consistency vs. eventual consistency)

components.name: RateLimitingService
components.description: Distributed rate limiting engine that enforces tenant quotas and endpoint overrides across all API gateway nodes. Processes individual request decisions with sub-5ms p99 latency while maintaining consistent state through a hybrid caching strategy. Handles enforcement decisions based on cached configurations, not real-time quota tracking. Built as a stateless service to enable horizontal scaling without coordination overhead between gateway nodes.

components.name: TenantConfigurationManager
components.description: Dedicated component responsible for managing tenant configurations including base quotas and endpoint overrides. Provides event-driven updates to RateLimitingService via message broker. Maintains audit trail of configuration changes with version control and rollback capabilities. Implements authorization checks to ensure only authorized clients can modify tenant settings, explicitly validating that the tenant_id in OAuth2 token matches the tenant_id in request path.

components.name: TenantConfigurationStore
components.description: Distributed key-value store that caches tenant configurations including base quotas and endpoint overrides. Provides low-latency access to tenant settings with eventual consistency model for configuration updates. Maintains a cache hierarchy with local node cache and shared distributed cache to minimize round-trips while ensuring configuration availability during partial outages. Serves as the source of truth for rate-limiting decisions without becoming a bottleneck. Uses encryption at rest via AWS KMS.

components.name: QuotaTracker
components.description: Distributed counter system that tracks per-tenant request consumption in real-time across all gateway nodes using probabilistic algorithms with local counters and batched updates to Redis. Implements sliding window algorithm with time-based tracking to enforce precise rate limits while maintaining sub-5ms p99 latency for decision processing. Uses a hybrid approach where 95% of quota decisions are made locally, with periodic synchronization to Redis for consistency checks.

components.name: APIGateway
components.description: Stateless API gateway that receives incoming requests and makes real-time decisions about rate limiting using gRPC streaming connections to RateLimitingService. Performs lightweight rate-limiting checks against local cache before forwarding requests to backend services. Does not maintain any persistent state or coordination with other gateways, enabling horizontal scaling without single points of failure. Communicates with RateLimitingService for configuration lookups and quota validation using gRPC streaming with mutual TLS authentication.

components.name: MessageBroker
components.description: Event-driven message broker that facilitates communication between TenantConfigurationManager and RateLimitingService. Ensures reliable delivery of configuration updates and maintains ordering guarantees for tenant settings changes. Used to broadcast configuration updates to all rate-limiting service instances in a consistent manner.

components.name: ConfigurationCache
components.description: Dedicated caching layer that maintains synchronized copies of tenant configurations across all API gateway nodes. Implements deterministic cache warming strategy with TTL values for different data types, ensuring consistency within 100ms of configuration changes. Handles cache invalidation through message broker events and periodic refreshes to maintain accurate quota settings.

architecture.infrastructure: Distributed Redis cluster with read replicas for TenantConfigurationStore, stateless service containers deployed across multiple availability zones with auto-scaling based on request volume, API gateway nodes configured as lightweight stateless proxies with no persistent coordination requirements. All components designed for horizontal scaling without single points of failure while maintaining sub-5ms p99 latency target for rate-limiting decisions. Uses AWS ElastiCache for Redis with memory optimization to reduce costs and improve performance. Multiple redundant API gateways deployed across availability zones with automatic failover capabilities.

decisions.decision: Use distributed Redis cluster for shared state management
decisions.alternatives_considered: Redis Cluster vs. DynamoDB vs. PostgreSQL with sharding
decisions.trade_offs: Redis provides sub-millisecond latency for key-value operations while maintaining eventual consistency model that tolerates partial outages. DynamoDB offers managed scaling but introduces vendor lock-in and higher latency for complex operations. PostgreSQL would require complex sharding and introduce transactional overhead not needed for rate-limiting decisions.
decisions.rationale: The Redis cluster approach provides the required sub-5ms p99 performance target while maintaining horizontal scalability without single points of failure. The eventual consistency model is acceptable for rate-limiting decisions where slight timing variations are tolerable compared to the performance benefits. AWS ElastiCache with memory optimization reduces costs while maintaining performance.

decisions.decision: Implement sliding window algorithm with time-based tracking
decisions.alternatives_considered: Fixed window vs. sliding window vs. token bucket
decisions.trade_offs: Sliding window provides more accurate rate limiting than fixed window while avoiding complex state management of token bucket. Fixed window is simpler but introduces bursty behavior and unfair allocation. Token bucket requires maintaining per-tenant state that increases complexity.
decisions.rationale: The sliding window algorithm provides the most precise rate limiting behavior required for a multi-tenant platform where fair distribution of resources across tenants is critical. Time-based tracking ensures consistency without requiring coordination between nodes. Implemented using probabilistic algorithms with local counters and batched updates to Redis.

decisions.decision: Use hybrid approach with local caching and periodic synchronization
decisions.alternatives_considered: Local-only vs. distributed counters vs. hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Local-only approach introduces inconsistency during configuration changes. Distributed counters create bottleneck at scale. Hybrid approach balances performance with consistency.
decisions.rationale: The hybrid approach achieves required sub-5ms p99 performance while maintaining scalability across thousands of concurrent tenants. 95% of quota decisions are made locally with periodic synchronization to Redis for consistency checks, reducing Redis dependency to configuration lookups only.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Stateful gateways vs. stateless gateways vs. hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Stateful gateways would create single points of failure and coordination overhead. Stateless design enables horizontal scaling without complex coordination but requires shared state management. Hybrid approaches add complexity without clear benefits.
decisions.rationale: The stateless gateway design eliminates single points of failure while enabling horizontal scaling to handle 500K requests/sec load target. The rate-limiting service handles all shared state management, allowing gateways to make decisions without maintaining persistent coordination with other nodes.

decisions.decision: Separate configuration management from enforcement engine
decisions.alternatives_considered: Monolithic approach vs. separation of concerns
decisions.trade_offs: Monolithic approach simplifies implementation but increases coupling and reduces maintainability. Separation of concerns improves modularity, testability, and reduces risk of inconsistent behavior when configurations change.
decisions.rationale: Separating configuration management from enforcement ensures clear ownership of responsibilities and reduces coupling between components. This prevents potential inconsistencies in behavior when tenant settings are updated and makes the system more maintainable.

decisions.decision: Use gRPC streaming for communication between gateways and rate-limiting service
decisions.alternatives_considered: gRPC streaming vs. HTTP/REST vs. WebSocket
decisions.trade_offs: gRPC streaming provides sub-millisecond latency with persistent connections, eliminating HTTP overhead. HTTP/REST is lightweight but introduces connection overhead. WebSocket provides real-time communication but violates stateless design.
decisions.rationale: gRPC streaming enables sub-millisecond latency for rate-limiting decisions while maintaining the stateless gateway architecture. Persistent connections reduce overhead compared to HTTP/REST calls and eliminate the performance bottleneck of synchronous HTTP calls.

security_controls.threat_model_summary: A malicious tenant could exhaust their quota faster than intended by making repeated rapid requests to exploit window boundary timing; an attacker could spoof a tenant's identity to bypass rate limits by forging request headers; a compromised gateway node could cache invalid quota data and allow excessive requests; a DoS attack on the Redis cluster could block all rate-limiting decisions, causing service degradation; a platform operator with access to configuration APIs could manipulate tenant quotas to cause unfair resource allocation or denial of service for other tenants.
security_controls.authentication: APIGateway nodes authenticate to RateLimitingService via mTLS with short-lived certificates issued by a managed PKI (e.g., AWS PCA or HashiCorp Vault), validated at the service boundary. Tenant configuration APIs use OAuth2 with client credentials grant type, where each tenant's API client is provisioned with a unique client ID and secret stored in a managed secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager). All tokens have 1-hour lifetime with automatic refresh via a secure token exchange endpoint. Each OAuth2 token includes a custom claim binding the client to a specific tenant_id to prevent credential impersonation. Explicit validation ensures that the tenant_id from the OAuth2 token matches the tenant_id in the request path.
security_controls.authorization: RBAC model for platform ops users with roles: 'admin' (full access), 'viewer' (read-only), and 'tenant-manager' (limited to their own tenant's configuration). Tenant API endpoints use ownership-based authorization where each tenant can only modify their own quota settings, enforced at the service boundary. Explicit authorization checks verify that the authenticated OAuth2 client is authorized to act on behalf of the specified tenant using a mapping stored in the TenantConfigurationStore. Explicit ownership checks ensure that users cannot modify configurations for tenants they don't own.
security_controls.iam: Services use managed identities for AWS (or equivalent cloud provider) with least-privilege policies: RateLimitingService has read/write access to Redis cluster and read-only access to secrets store; APIGateway uses read-only access to Redis cluster for quota lookups; TenantConfigurationStore uses read/write permissions to Redis cluster. All service-to-service communication is secured via mTLS or cloud provider-managed identity federation.
security_controls.network_boundaries: Zero Trust perimeter with all internal communications secured by mTLS between services and enforced by cloud provider security groups (AWS SGs) that restrict traffic to only necessary ports and IP ranges. Public API entry point is through multiple redundant API Gateways (AWS API Gateway or equivalent) that terminate TLS, rate-limits at the edge, and forwards requests to stateless gateway nodes. Internal service-to-service communication occurs within a private VPC with no public internet access.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 90 days for API client credentials and mTLS certificates. TLS in transit uses TLS 1.3 with enforced cipher suites (no legacy protocols). No data at rest encryption is required as the system only tracks request counts and configuration metadata, not sensitive personal or financial information. Automated secret rotation and revocation workflows implemented using AWS Secrets Manager's event-driven triggers. Redis cluster enabled with encryption at rest using AWS KMS.

reliability_design.scaling_strategy: The primary scaling bottleneck is the QuotaTracker component, which handles atomic increment operations on distributed counters for each tenant. Horizontal autoscaling is implemented on APIGateway nodes based on request rate metrics (requests per second) to distribute load across the system. The Redis cluster serves as the shared state layer and scales horizontally via sharding with read replicas to handle concurrent counter updates. Each gateway node maintains a local LRU cache of recent tenant quotas for sub-5ms p99 latency decisions, reducing dependency on distributed state for frequently accessed tenants.
reliability_design.reliability: The system uses circuit breaker pattern around the Redis cluster for quota tracking and configuration store to prevent cascading failures during partial outages. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter is implemented for transient Redis connectivity issues. Bulkhead isolation ensures that a single tenant's quota exhaustion or misconfiguration doesn't impact other tenants' rate-limiting decisions. Timeout budgets of 2ms are enforced on all distributed calls to prevent slow Redis operations from causing request queuing. When Redis is unavailable, the system defaults to allowing requests with warning log entries for alerting purposes, but implements a grace period mechanism where requests are allowed but logged for immediate alerting if Redis becomes unavailable for more than 5 seconds. Redis shards are distributed using consistent hashing to prevent hot shard issues.
reliability_design.disaster_recovery: Multi-site active-active strategy using AWS ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ support and sub-1-minute RTO. Automated failover is implemented across regions with Redis Active-Active replication. RTO is reduced from 10-15 minutes to under 5 minutes, aligning with the 99.99% availability target. Backup frequency is incremental every 5 minutes, providing an RPO of maximum 5 minutes of data loss. Multiple redundant API gateways deployed across availability zones with automatic failover capabilities.
reliability_design.observability: Traces cover the critical API gateway to RateLimitingService decision path with sampling rate of 100% for all requests. Metrics include request rate per tenant, p99 latency distribution for quota checks, Redis cluster health indicators, and cache hit ratios. Structured logs capture RequestDecision entities with tenant_id, endpoint_path, allowed status, and quota_used details for audit and debugging purposes. SLOs defined: '99.9% of rate-limiting decisions must complete within 2ms' and '99.99% of quota lookups must succeed'. Alerts set up based on these metrics with appropriate thresholds (e.g., p99 latency > 3ms triggers alert).
failure_scenarios: Redis cluster becomes unavailable: Circuit breaker trips, requests are allowed with warning log entries and immediate alerting if unavailability exceeds 5 seconds, system continues operating at reduced enforcement fidelity but maintains availability
API gateway node fails: No impact on rate-limiting service or shared state, other gateways continue processing requests without coordination overhead
Tenant configuration store becomes slow: Local cache in API gateways provides fallback for 10-30 second window while configuration is refreshed from distributed store
Quota tracker counter update fails: Atomic increment operation retries with jitter, system allows request and logs error for alerting purposes
Network partition between gateway and rate-limiting service: Gateway uses cached quota configurations for up to 2 seconds before requiring fresh data
Hot shard issue in Redis cluster: Circuit breaker and retry logic isolate shard failures, consistent hashing distributes load across multiple shards
Multiple API gateways fail: Automatic failover to redundant gateways ensures continued operation without service disruption

findings.issue: OAuth2 client credentials tokens are validated only at the API gateway boundary, but there is no mechanism to prevent a compromised or misconfigured gateway node from caching invalid tenant quota data and allowing excessive requests.
findings.recommendation: Implement a token revocation mechanism (e.g., JWT blacklisting or short-lived tokens with frequent refresh) in the TenantConfigurationManager to invalidate stale or compromised tokens. Additionally, add a cryptographic signature validation step on all configuration updates received from the TenantConfigurationManager to ensure that only authorized and authenticated sources can modify tenant settings.

findings.issue: The authorization check for tenant configuration APIs explicitly validates that the tenant_id in the OAuth2 token matches the tenant_id in the request path, but does not validate whether the authenticated client has been granted permission to act on behalf of that tenant. This could allow an attacker with access to a valid client credential to impersonate any tenant if they can guess or brute-force tenant IDs.
findings.recommendation: Add an explicit mapping check in the TenantConfigurationManager between OAuth2 clients and tenants, ensuring that each client is explicitly bound to one or more specific tenant IDs. This prevents a single compromised client from accessing configurations for multiple tenants.

findings.issue: While mTLS is used between services, the design does not specify how service identities are managed or rotated, which introduces risk of credential leakage and prolonged exposure if certificates are not properly rotated.
findings.recommendation: Implement a certificate lifecycle management system with automated rotation (e.g., using AWS PCA or HashiCorp Vault) that enforces short certificate lifetimes (e.g., 30 days) and includes a mechanism to revoke compromised certificates immediately.

findings.issue: The design states that no data at rest encryption is required because the system only tracks request counts and configuration metadata, not sensitive personal or financial information. However, it does not address potential exposure of quota data through cache invalidation or misconfiguration scenarios where cached values might be exposed.
findings.recommendation: Add a mechanism to sanitize or clear local caches upon any configuration change or during certificate rotation to prevent accidental exposure of stale quota information. Also, implement strict access controls on all caching layers to ensure only authorized processes can read cached data.

findings.issue: The system uses a hybrid approach with local caching and periodic synchronization to Redis, but there's no mechanism described for handling cache inconsistency during network partitions or Redis failures that could lead to unauthorized access due to stale quota data.
findings.recommendation: Implement a cache consistency protocol that includes a fallback behavior when Redis is unavailable (e.g., default to allowing requests with immediate alerting) and ensures that any cached data is invalidated or refreshed upon detection of network issues or Redis unavailability.

findings.issue: The Redis cluster (ElastiCache) is the primary cost driver at ~$10,000/month for 500K requests/sec with 95% local caching and 5% Redis sync. This assumes 200+ Redis shards with read replicas to handle concurrent counter updates and maintain sub-5ms latency.
findings.recommendation: Validate the actual Redis shard count needed - current estimate assumes high concurrency that may not be required at scale, but also doesn't account for burst traffic spikes that could drive costs higher.

findings.issue: The design doesn't account for data egress from Redis cluster to API gateways. With 500K requests/sec and 5% hitting Redis, this could easily exceed $2,000/month in egress fees depending on region and network topology.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit egress cost modeling for the Redis cluster to gateway communications.

findings.issue: The $15,000 budget must cover monitoring, alerting, and operational costs beyond raw infrastructure - this is not explicitly modeled in the estimate.
findings.recommendation: Budget should include at least $1,000/month for observability tools (e.g., Datadog, New Relic) and alerting systems.

findings.issue: The design claims a 99.99% availability target (allowing 53 minutes/year downtime) but the disaster recovery strategy specifies an RTO of <5 minutes for multi-site active-active Redis failover, which exceeds the allowable downtime budget.
findings.recommendation: Reduce the claimed RTO to align with the 99.99% availability target. Either implement a backup-and-restore or pilot-light DR strategy with RTO <53 minutes, or increase the availability target to 99.999% (allowing ~5.3 minutes/year downtime) to justify the stated <5 minute RTO. The current DR strategy cannot meet the 99.99% SLA.

findings.issue: The design states that APIGateway nodes are stateless and do not coordinate with each other, but does not specify how the system handles tenant configuration changes when a gateway node fails before receiving an update from the message broker. This creates a potential SPOF in configuration propagation.
findings.recommendation: Implement a mechanism for configuration updates to be cached locally on each gateway node with TTL-based refreshes, or ensure that configuration updates are broadcast via multiple channels (e.g., both message broker and direct cache invalidation) to prevent configuration staleness during gateway failures.

findings.issue: The design claims to use circuit breakers around Redis but does not specify timeout values or retry policies for the gRPC streaming connections between API Gateway and RateLimitingService. Without explicit timeouts, a slow downstream service could cause request queuing and violate the 2ms timeout budget.
findings.recommendation: Specify explicit timeout values (e.g., 100ms) on gRPC streaming calls to RateLimitingService with retry policies including jitter and circuit breaker thresholds. Ensure that all service-to-service communication enforces timeout budgets to prevent cascading failures.

findings.issue: The SLOs are defined but not clearly linked to alerting thresholds. The design states 'p99 latency > 3ms triggers alert' but this is inconsistent with the stated 2ms timeout budget for quota checks, which would make any alerting based on 3ms p99 potentially too lenient.
findings.recommendation: Align SLO thresholds with the 2ms p99 latency requirement. Define alerting thresholds at or below 2ms p99 to ensure that performance degradation is caught before it impacts availability. The current threshold of 3ms may allow degraded performance to persist undetected.

findings.issue: The design relies on eventual consistency for configuration updates, but does not specify how the system handles cases where a gateway node has cached an old configuration and continues to enforce it after a new configuration is applied. This could lead to inconsistent rate-limiting enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Implement cache invalidation with deterministic TTL values or versioned configurations that gateways must validate against before applying changes. Add explicit cache warming strategies during node startup and configuration updates to ensure consistency.

findings.issue: The hybrid caching approach with local counters and batched Redis updates introduces a critical race condition where concurrent requests from the same tenant can be processed with inconsistent quota state. The system assumes 95% of decisions are made locally, but there's no mechanism to prevent two gateways from simultaneously incrementing a counter in their local cache before the next batch update to Redis.
findings.recommendation: Implement a distributed atomic counter pattern using Redis Lua scripts for all quota increments, or switch to a fully synchronous approach for quota updates. Eliminate the hybrid approach entirely - if you're going to use local counters, ensure they're synchronized atomically with Redis on every increment, not batched. Alternatively, abandon local counters and use only Redis-based tracking with proper sharding and connection pooling to maintain sub-5ms latency.

findings.issue: The APIGateway nodes depend on gRPC streaming connections to RateLimitingService for configuration lookups, but the architecture doesn't account for what happens when the RateLimitingService becomes unavailable or slow. The system assumes gateways can fall back to cached configurations, but the design lacks a clear timeout and fallback strategy that would prevent cascading failures across all gateway nodes.
findings.recommendation: Implement a circuit breaker with aggressive timeouts (1-2ms) on gRPC streaming connections from gateways to RateLimitingService. Add a 'last known good' cache that persists for at least 30 seconds beyond the last successful update, and implement a hard fallback policy where requests are allowed if the service is unresponsive for more than 50ms, with immediate alerting and logging for ops teams.

findings.area: Assumptions that don't hold at stated scale
findings.issue: The sliding window algorithm implemented with probabilistic local counters assumes that tenants have a uniform distribution of requests, but the brief states 'thousands of tenants' with 500K requests/sec. At this scale, even a small number of highly active tenants can cause Redis hotspots due to the distributed nature of the counter updates, creating a bottleneck that will exceed the 5ms p99 requirement.
findings.recommendation: Replace the probabilistic local counters with a Redis-based sliding window implementation using sorted sets or time-series data structures. This ensures consistent performance regardless of tenant activity distribution and prevents hot shard issues. The local cache should only be used for configuration lookups, not quota tracking.

findings.issue: The architecture is overengineered for the stated $15K/month budget and 500K RPS load. Using a Redis cluster with read replicas, multiple availability zones, and complex caching hierarchies is unnecessary when the system only needs to track request counts and simple configurations. The design introduces operational complexity that exceeds what can be maintained within the budget constraints.
findings.recommendation: Simplify to a single Redis instance with read replicas for high availability, or better yet, use a managed service like AWS ElastiCache with auto-scaling that's designed for this type of workload. Eliminate the complex cache hierarchy and deterministic warming strategy - these add operational overhead without meaningful benefit at this scale.

findings.issue: The architecture uses gRPC streaming for communication between gateways and RateLimitingService, but the brief explicitly requires 'sub-5ms p99 latency' for rate-limiting decisions. gRPC streaming introduces connection establishment overhead and is not designed for high-frequency, low-latency decision-making. The system needs to process 500K requests/sec, which means every millisecond counts.
findings.recommendation: Replace gRPC streaming with HTTP/1.1 or even UDP-based approach for rate-limiting decisions. Use a connection pool with pre-established connections and implement a highly optimized HTTP client that can handle the required throughput without connection overhead. The streaming protocol is inappropriate for this use case and will introduce unnecessary latency.

findings.issue: The QuotaTracker component and the TenantConfigurationStore both appear to manage tenant quota data, but their responsibilities are not clearly separated. The QuotaTracker claims to track 'per-tenant request consumption in real-time' while the TenantConfigurationStore is described as a 'distributed key-value store that caches tenant configurations'. This overlap creates ambiguity about where actual quota tracking happens.
findings.recommendation: Clearly define the responsibilities: TenantConfigurationStore should only manage configuration data (base quotas, endpoint overrides) and TenantQuota should be managed exclusively by a dedicated QuotaTrackingService that handles the actual counting logic. Remove the dual responsibility from QuotaTracker.

findings.area: Hedged decisions dressed up as thorough ones
findings.issue: The hybrid approach between local counters and Redis updates is presented as 'thorough' but is actually a half-decision that fails to address fundamental scalability issues. The system claims to maintain sub-5ms p99 latency while also claiming to handle 500K requests/sec, which is impossible without either significant hardware resources or architectural changes.
findings.recommendation: Make a clear decision: either use fully synchronous quota tracking with Redis for consistency and reliability (accepting some performance trade-offs), or abandon local counters entirely and rely on Redis-based tracking. The current hybrid approach is a design flaw that will cause operational issues at scale.

architecture_stages.characteristics: A simplified, single-region implementation that validates core rate-limiting functionality with minimal infrastructure and operational overhead. Focuses on proving the basic quota enforcement model while maintaining the essential architectural principles of distributed state management and stateless gateways.

architecture_stages.characteristics: Multi-region deployment with read replicas, horizontal autoscaling capability, and enhanced monitoring while maintaining the core hybrid caching architecture. Introduces message queue for configuration updates and implements more robust circuit breaker patterns.
architecture_stages.purpose: Scale to handle increased tenant load and traffic volume while improving reliability and operational efficiency
architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When system experiences sustained request rate of 200,000 requests/sec across all tenants or when latency exceeds 5ms p99 for more than 1% of requests during peak hours

architecture_stages.transition_trigger: When system reaches 500,000 requests/sec across all tenants or when compliance requirements mandate regional data residency for specific tenant segments

security_controls.threat_model_summary: A malicious tenant could exhaust their quota faster than intended by making repeated rapid requests to exploit window boundary timing; an attacker could spoof a tenant's identity to bypass rate limits by forging request headers; a compromised gateway node could cache invalid quota data and allow excessive requests; a DoS attack on the Redis cluster could block all rate-limiting decisions, causing service degradation; a platform operator with access to configuration APIs could manipulate tenant quotas to cause unfair resource allocation or denial of service for other tenants.
security_controls.authentication: APIGateway nodes authenticate to RateLimitingService via mTLS with short-lived certificates issued by a managed PKI (e.g., AWS PCA or HashiCorp Vault), validated at the service boundary. Tenant configuration APIs use OAuth2 with client credentials grant type, where each tenant's API client is provisioned with a unique client ID and secret stored in a managed secrets store (AWS Secrets Manager). All tokens have 1-hour lifetime with automatic refresh via a secure token exchange endpoint. Each OAuth2 token includes a custom claim binding the client to a specific tenant_id to prevent credential impersonation. Explicit validation ensures that the tenant_id from the OAuth2 token matches the tenant_id in the request path.
security_controls.authorization: RBAC model for platform ops users with roles: 'admin' (full access), 'viewer' (read-only), and 'tenant-manager' (limited to their own tenant's configuration). Tenant API endpoints use ownership-based authorization where each tenant can only modify their own quota settings, enforced at the service boundary. Explicit authorization checks verify that the authenticated OAuth2 client is authorized to act on behalf of the specified tenant using a mapping stored in the TenantConfigurationStore. Explicit ownership checks ensure that users cannot modify configurations for tenants they don't own.
security_controls.iam: Services use managed identities for AWS (or equivalent cloud provider) with least-privilege policies: RateLimitingService has read/write access to Redis cluster and read-only access to secrets store; APIGateway uses read-only access to Redis cluster for quota lookups; TenantConfigurationStore uses read/write permissions to Redis cluster. All service-to-service communication is secured via mTLS or cloud provider-managed identity federation.
security_controls.network_boundaries: Zero Trust perimeter with all internal communications secured by mTLS between services and enforced by cloud provider security groups (AWS SGs) that restrict traffic to only necessary ports and IP ranges. Public API entry point is through multiple redundant API Gateways (AWS API Gateway or equivalent) that terminate TLS, rate-limits at the edge, and forwards requests to stateless gateway nodes. Internal service-to-service communication occurs within a private VPC with no public internet access.
security_controls.secrets_and_encryption: All secrets managed via AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation every 90 days for API client credentials and mTLS certificates. TLS in transit uses TLS 1.3 with enforced cipher suites (no legacy protocols). No data at rest encryption is required as the system only tracks request counts and configuration metadata, not sensitive personal or financial information. Automated secret rotation and revocation workflows implemented using AWS Secrets Manager's event-driven triggers. Redis cluster enabled with encryption at rest using AWS KMS.

threats.issue: OAuth2 client credentials tokens are validated only at the API gateway boundary, but there is no mechanism to prevent a compromised or misconfigured gateway node from caching invalid tenant quota data and allowing excessive requests.
threats.recommendation: Implement a token revocation mechanism (e.g., JWT blacklisting or short-lived tokens with frequent refresh) in the TenantConfigurationManager to invalidate stale or compromised tokens. Additionally, add a cryptographic signature validation step on all configuration updates received from the TenantConfigurationManager to ensure that only authorized and authenticated sources can modify tenant settings.

threats.issue: The authorization check for tenant configuration APIs explicitly validates that the tenant_id in the OAuth2 token matches the tenant_id in the request path, but does not validate whether the authenticated client has been granted permission to act on behalf of that tenant. This could allow an attacker with access to a valid client credential to impersonate any tenant if they can guess or brute-force tenant IDs.
threats.recommendation: Add an explicit mapping check in the TenantConfigurationManager between OAuth2 clients and tenants, ensuring that each client is explicitly bound to one or more specific tenant IDs. This prevents a single compromised client from accessing configurations for multiple tenants.

threats.issue: While mTLS is used between services, the design does not specify how service identities are managed or rotated, which introduces risk of credential leakage and prolonged exposure if certificates are not properly rotated.
threats.recommendation: Implement a certificate lifecycle management system with automated rotation (e.g., using AWS PCA or HashiCorp Vault) that enforces short certificate lifetimes (e.g., 30 days) and includes a mechanism to revoke compromised certificates immediately.

threats.issue: The design states that no data at rest encryption is required because the system only tracks request counts and configuration metadata, not sensitive personal or financial information. However, it does not address potential exposure of quota data through cache invalidation or misconfiguration scenarios where cached values might be exposed.
threats.recommendation: Add a mechanism to sanitize or clear local caches upon any configuration change or during certificate rotation to prevent accidental exposure of stale quota information. Also, implement strict access controls on all caching layers to ensure only authorized processes can read cached data.

threats.issue: The system uses a hybrid approach with local caching and periodic synchronization to Redis, but there's no mechanism described for handling cache inconsistency during network partitions or Redis failures that could lead to unauthorized access due to stale quota data.
threats.recommendation: Implement a cache consistency protocol that includes a fallback behavior when Redis is unavailable (e.g., default to allowing requests with immediate alerting) and ensures that any cached data is invalidated or refreshed upon detection of network issues or Redis unavailability.

blueprint.infrastructure: Distributed Redis cluster with read replicas for TenantConfigurationStore, stateless service containers deployed across multiple availability zones with auto-scaling based on request volume, API gateway nodes configured as lightweight stateless proxies with no persistent coordination requirements. All components designed for horizontal scaling without single points of failure while maintaining sub-5ms p99 latency target for rate-limiting decisions. Uses AWS ElastiCache for Redis with memory optimization to reduce costs and improve performance. Multiple redundant API gateways deployed across availability zones with automatic failover capabilities.
blueprint.scaling_strategy: The primary scaling bottleneck is the QuotaTracker component, which handles atomic increment operations on distributed counters for each tenant. Horizontal autoscaling is implemented on APIGateway nodes based on request rate metrics (requests per second) to distribute load across the system. The Redis cluster serves as the shared state layer and scales horizontally via sharding with read replicas to handle concurrent counter updates. Each gateway node maintains a local LRU cache of recent tenant quotas for sub-5ms p99 latency decisions, reducing dependency on distributed state for frequently accessed tenants.
blueprint.reliability: The system uses circuit breaker pattern around the Redis cluster for quota tracking and configuration store to prevent cascading failures during partial outages. Retry with exponential backoff and jitter is implemented for transient Redis connectivity issues. Bulkhead isolation ensures that a single tenant's quota exhaustion or misconfiguration doesn't impact other tenants' rate-limiting decisions. Timeout budgets of 2ms are enforced on all distributed calls to prevent slow Redis operations from causing request queuing. When Redis is unavailable, the system defaults to allowing requests with warning log entries for alerting purposes, but implements a grace period mechanism where requests are allowed but logged for immediate alerting if Redis becomes unavailable for more than 5 seconds. Redis shards are distributed using consistent hashing to prevent hot shard issues.
blueprint.disaster_recovery: Multi-site active-active strategy using AWS ElastiCache for Redis with Multi-AZ support and sub-1-minute RTO. Automated failover is implemented across regions with Redis Active-Active replication. RTO is reduced from 10-15 minutes to under 5 minutes, aligning with the 99.99% availability target. Backup frequency is incremental every 5 minutes, providing an RPO of maximum 5 minutes of data loss. Multiple redundant API gateways deployed across availability zones with automatic failover capabilities.
blueprint.observability: Traces cover the critical API gateway to RateLimitingService decision path with sampling rate of 100% for all requests. Metrics include request rate per tenant, p99 latency distribution for quota checks, Redis cluster health indicators, and cache hit ratios. Structured logs capture RequestDecision entities with tenant_id, endpoint_path, allowed status, and quota_used details for audit and debugging purposes. SLOs defined: '99.9% of rate-limiting decisions must complete within 2ms' and '99.99% of quota lookups must succeed'. Alerts set up based on these metrics with appropriate thresholds (e.g., p99 latency > 3ms triggers alert).
failure_scenarios: Redis cluster becomes unavailable: Circuit breaker trips, requests are allowed with warning log entries and immediate alerting if unavailability exceeds 5 seconds, system continues operating at reduced enforcement fidelity but maintains availability
API gateway node fails: No impact on rate-limiting service or shared state, other gateways continue processing requests without coordination overhead
Tenant configuration store becomes slow: Local cache in API gateways provides fallback for 10-30 second window while configuration is refreshed from distributed store
Quota tracker counter update fails: Atomic increment operation retries with jitter, system allows request and logs error for alerting purposes
Network partition between gateway and rate-limiting service: Gateway uses cached quota configurations for up to 2 seconds before requiring fresh data
Hot shard issue in Redis cluster: Circuit breaker and retry logic isolate shard failures, consistent hashing distributes load across multiple shards
Multiple API gateways fail: Automatic failover to redundant gateways ensures continued operation without service disruption

decisions.decision: Use distributed Redis cluster for shared state management
decisions.alternatives_considered: Redis Cluster vs. DynamoDB vs. PostgreSQL with sharding
decisions.trade_offs: Redis provides sub-millisecond latency for key-value operations while maintaining eventual consistency model that tolerates partial outages. DynamoDB offers managed scaling but introduces vendor lock-in and higher latency for complex operations. PostgreSQL would require complex sharding and introduce transactional overhead not needed for rate-limiting decisions.
decisions.rationale: The Redis cluster approach provides the required sub-5ms p99 performance target while maintaining horizontal scalability without single points of failure. The eventual consistency model is acceptable for rate-limiting decisions where slight timing variations are tolerable compared to the performance benefits. AWS ElastiCache with memory optimization reduces costs while maintaining performance.

decisions.decision: Implement sliding window algorithm with time-based tracking
decisions.alternatives_considered: Fixed window vs. sliding window vs. token bucket
decisions.trade_offs: Sliding window provides more accurate rate limiting than fixed window while avoiding complex state management of token bucket. Fixed window is simpler but introduces bursty behavior and unfair allocation. Token bucket requires maintaining per-tenant state that increases complexity.
decisions.rationale: The sliding window algorithm provides the most precise rate limiting behavior required for a multi-tenant platform where fair distribution of resources across tenants is critical. Time-based tracking ensures consistency without requiring coordination between nodes. Implemented using probabilistic algorithms with local counters and batched updates to Redis.

decisions.decision: Use hybrid approach with local caching and periodic synchronization
decisions.alternatives_considered: Local-only vs. distributed counters vs. hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Local-only approach introduces inconsistency during configuration changes. Distributed counters create bottleneck at scale. Hybrid approach balances performance with consistency.
decisions.rationale: The hybrid approach achieves required sub-5ms p99 performance while maintaining scalability across thousands of concurrent tenants. 95% of quota decisions are made locally with periodic synchronization to Redis for consistency checks, reducing Redis dependency to configuration lookups only.

decisions.alternatives_considered: Stateful gateways vs. stateless gateways vs. hybrid approach
decisions.trade_offs: Stateful gateways would create single points of failure and coordination overhead. Stateless design enables horizontal scaling without complex coordination but requires shared state management. Hybrid approaches add complexity without clear benefits.
decisions.rationale: The stateless gateway design eliminates single points of failure while enabling horizontal scaling to handle 500K requests/sec load target. The rate-limiting service handles all shared state management, allowing gateways to make decisions without maintaining persistent coordination with other nodes.

decisions.decision: Separate configuration management from enforcement engine
decisions.alternatives_considered: Monolithic approach vs. separation of concerns
decisions.trade_offs: Monolithic approach simplifies implementation but increases coupling and reduces maintainability. Separation of concerns improves modularity, testability, and reduces risk of inconsistent behavior when configurations change.
decisions.rationale: Separating configuration management from enforcement ensures clear ownership of responsibilities and reduces coupling between components. This prevents potential inconsistencies in behavior when tenant settings are updated and makes the system more maintainable.

decisions.decision: Use gRPC streaming for communication between gateways and rate-limiting service
decisions.alternatives_considered: gRPC streaming vs. HTTP/REST vs. WebSocket
decisions.trade_offs: gRPC streaming provides sub-millisecond latency with persistent connections, eliminating HTTP overhead. HTTP/REST is lightweight but introduces connection overhead. WebSocket provides real-time communication but violates stateless design.
decisions.rationale: gRPC streaming enables sub-millisecond latency for rate-limiting decisions while maintaining the stateless gateway architecture. Persistent connections reduce overhead compared to HTTP/REST calls and eliminate the performance bottleneck of synchronous HTTP calls.
